h: What you will do in this tutorial
x: A hands-on, step-by-step guide. You start with what an ontology is, then connect source databases, query data with Cypher, build an ontology with an agent, run actions on business systems, and finally build apps on top of it all. What you will do in this tutorial Ontological Studio is a desktop program for building ontologies, running queries and actions, and building business apps . A single installer includes a graph database (Ontological DB), a data fabric, an ontology-building agent, an action executor and sample business systems, so you can do every exercise from start to finish on one laptop. This tutorial follows the supply chain operations of one company. The company's data is spread across three systems. System Data Example Purchasing ERP ( erp ) Suppliers, items, purchase orders, order lines We ordered 2,000 PCB boards from Shenzhen Goldline PCB Logistics WMS ( wms ) Inbound shipments, daily stock A shipment for that order has been held at customs for 9 days Customer CRM ( crm ) Customers, sales orders, claims A customer in Tokyo filed a PCB soldering defect claim To answer “Which inbound shipments are more than 3 days late, and which supplier and purchase order are they for?”, you have to connect data from all three systems. By the end of the tutorial you will answer this question with a graph query, carry out the instruction “Expedite those shipments” on the real systems after an approval step, and build a business app that brings all of this together on one screen. Learning path 1 · Getting started Install, first run, a tour of the app 2 · Ontology concepts Classes, properties, relationships, instances; how the app is built 3 · Connecting data Source databases as virtual nodes, without copying 4 · Learning Cypher From MATCH to aggregation, diagnostics and time travel 5 · Building the ontology Golden Questions and Golden Commands, building from documents, querying 6 · Actions Registering systems, creating actions, approve, execute, cancel 7 · Applications Dashboards, code apps, the SDK, action buttons 8 · Final project A hands-on project that uses everything you learned Each chapter goes concept → Try it → Check yourself . The answers to the Check yourself questions are folded, so try them on your own first, then open the answers. Who this tutorial is for If you have learned SQL SELECT and JOIN in a university database course, you are ready. You don't need to know graph databases or Cypher. Part 4 teaches them from scratch. You need a little programming only in Part 7 (code apps). Even there the agent writes the code, so being able to read it is enough. What you need Item Details Computer macOS (Apple Silicon M1 or later, or Intel) or Windows 10/11 (x64), 8 GB of memory recommended Disk At least 2 GB free Coding agent Claude Code or Codex CLI. If you install one and sign in, the build and query agents work without an API key. Without one, you can still do Parts 3 and 4 (connecting data, Cypher) as written. Network Needed only to download the installer and to use the agent (LLM). All databases run on your own computer. Prefer to watch first? The product page has demo videos of building from documents, creating actions from Golden Commands, and building ontology apps. This tutorial walks through those same steps one at a time. Conventions Text you type is in monospace, like MATCH (s:Supplier) RETURN s.name . Button names on screen are in bold, like Create virtual node . Screenshots use the light theme. A few demo shots in the dark theme are noted in their captions. Every number and result comes from actually running the sample data. h: The sample ontology at a glance
How is it different from tables?
Why AI agents need an ontology
x: Learn the four core concepts — class, property, relationship and instance — and use the sample to compare an ontology with handling data in tables. In one sentence An ontology is a model that defines the concepts your business needs and the relationships between them. Like an ER diagram, it describes the things in your business and how they relate. On top of that, you can connect real data to it and use it as the basis for queries and for carrying out work . Four core concepts Concept Description Example Class (node type, label) A kind of thing that appears in your business Supplier , PurchaseOrder , Shipment Property A value a class has Supplier.name , Shipment.delay_days Relationship A connection between two classes, with a direction and a name (PurchaseOrder)-[:ORDERED_FROM]->(Supplier) — a purchase order is placed with a supplier Instance (node) One piece of data that belongs to a class Supplier S-CN-01 Shenzhen Goldline PCB , purchase order PO-002 Classes and relationships are the schema ; instances and their connections are the data . In a graph database, instances are called nodes and connections are called edges (relationships) . The sample ontology at a glance Schema of the sample ontology “Supply Chain Operations (Sample)” — 7 classes and the relationships between them Class Description Source system Supplier Suppliers (5) ERP Item Items (4) ERP PurchaseOrder Purchase orders (8) ERP Shipment Inbound shipments (8) WMS Customer Customers (3) CRM SalesOrder Sales orders (5) CRM Claim Customer claims (3) CRM Relationship How to read it (Shipment)-[:SHIPS]->(PurchaseOrder) A shipment carries a purchase order (PurchaseOrder)-[:ORDERED_FROM]->(Supplier) A purchase order was placed with a supplier (SalesOrder)-[:PLACED_BY]->(Customer) A sales order was placed by a customer (SalesOrder)-[:FOR_ITEM]->(Item) A sales order is for an item (Claim)-[:ABOUT]->(SalesOrder) A claim is about a sales order (Shipment)-[:SHIPPED_BY]->(Supplier) A shipment was sent by a supplier (only in the built ontology — see Chapter 4 ) How is it different from tables? Let's compare SQL and a graph on the same question: “Which inbound shipments are more than 3 days late, and which supplier and purchase order are they for?” In SQL you join three tables. What's more, shipments live in WMS while purchase orders and suppliers live in ERP, so you would normally have to bring the two databases together first. In Cypher (a graph query language), you query connected data by relationship name. The join condition ( po.po_id = sh.ref_po_no ) is gone. What remains are SHIPS and ORDERED_FROM , the relationship names your business uses . You need to know the join keys only once, when you define the relationship. After that, people and AI agents alike only need to know the relationship names. An ontology pays off on the next question If you create a SQL view for each question, you get one more thing to maintain for every question. If you model entities and relationships instead, you can answer even a brand-new question by following relationships that already exist . Questions like “What are that supplier's other open purchase orders?” or “Which customers who bought that order's items filed a claim?” can be answered without any new design work. Why AI agents need an ontology Give an LLM agent the DDL for hundreds of tables, and every time it has to guess what a code name like TB507.C041 means and which columns to join on. An ontology settles those guesses once, in a form people have reviewed . Meaning — Shipment.delay_days comes with a description: “number of days past the expected arrival date”. Paths — the way from a shipment to its supplier is fixed by relationships. Behavior — what you can do to a shipment (“expedite”) and how to undo it are attached as actions (Part 6). That's why, in Ontological Studio, the same ontology is the basis for queries, for execution and for apps . Check yourself In the sample, which relationships, in which direction, do you follow to

Learn what each part of the app does and how data flows between them. This will help you see which parts you are using in the exercises that follow. Component map Component Role Ontological DB The graph database that stores ontologies and runs Cypher. It is a PostgreSQL extension, so graph queries are translated into PostgreSQL SQL and run there. It also handles bitemporal data (time travel), permissions and schema evolution. Data fabric A feature inside Ontological DB. It makes tables in other databases look like graph nodes without copying them (virtual nodes). Bolt gateway Supports Bolt, the protocol Neo4j uses. Studio and the Portal read and write the graph through it. Studio The ontology build, query and dashboard screens, and the agents behind them. Action executor Plans actions, evaluates policies, gets a person's approval, then calls the business system APIs. On cancel, it undoes the steps in reverse order. Sample business systems Purchasing ERP, Logistics WMS and Customer CRM: small REST services, each with its own authentication method. When an action calls them, values in the source databases change. There are two graphs Ontological DB can hold several graphs (separate data spaces). After a fresh install you will see two. Graph What it holds Mainly used for sample Virtual nodes and virtual relationships that expose the sample source tables as they are The Data Sources tab, Cypher exercises in the Portal (Part 4) ontology The ontology Studio built: class definitions, instances, relationships, action definitions Ask & Act, Ontology Apps (Parts 5–7) sample is “a mirror that shows the sources as they are”, and ontology is “knowledge organized from the business point of view”. For example, ontology has a SHIPPED_BY relationship (shipment → supplier) that the sources don't have, every class and property has a description, and actions are attached. Why keep them apart? Source table names and ontology class names are often the same ( Supplier ). If both lived in one graph, the read-only virtual nodes and the built nodes would collide. That's why the sample keeps its virtual nodes in a separate sample graph. The path of a question When the question “Which inbound shipments are more than 3 days late?” arrives in the Ask & Act tab: The agent reads the schema of the published ontology (which classes, relationships and properties exist). It writes Cypher and sends it to Ontological DB over Bolt. Ontological DB translates the Cypher into SQL and runs it. The data fabric passes the needed conditions down to the source databases. Along with the results, the answer states “which facts on which nodes it used as evidence”. The path of a command The command “Expedite those shipments” flows differently. The agent finds the action that fits this command ( Shipment.expediteShipment ). It asks the action executor for a plan . The executor picks the target shipments and, for each target, a policy decides whether to allow or deny it. Nothing has changed yet. A person approves it on the plan card. The executor calls the business system APIs in turn (change the priority in WMS → send an expedite request in ERP). The values in the source databases change, and because the data fabric reads them directly, the graph shows the change right away. If you say “Cancel what you just did”, the steps that succeeded are undone in reverse order (compensation). Neither agents nor apps call business systems directly. They always go through this executor. Check yourself You run MATCH (s:Supplier) RETURN s in the Portal. Connect a source database, explore its tables and columns, and preview its data without copying it. Along the way you will learn how the data fabric works. What is a data fabric? A company's data is spread across many databases. Usually it is copied (ETL) into a data warehouse, gathered in one place and analyzed there. A copy lags behind the original, permissions must be managed in two places, and whenever the original changes you have to copy it again. A data fabric leaves the data in the source and reads it each time you query. Ontological DB defines virtual nodes so you can query source tables as if they were graph nodes. It uses only definitions of nodes and relationships; the data itself is not copied. Copy (ETL) Data fabric Where the data is A copy in the warehouse Stays in the source Freshness As of the last load As of the moment you query Permissions Two places: source and copy One place: the source Writes Writing to the copy leaves the source unchanged Virtual nodes are read-only; writes go to the source system Opening the Data Sources tab On Home, click the Data Sources card. x: Turn erp.po_line (purchase order lines), a table that is not exposed yet, into a virtual node and connect it to purchase orders and items with relationships. You will practice linking tables from different databases into a single graph. What is a virtual node? A virtual node type defines one source table as a node type in the graph. One source row = one node , and columns = properties . The KEY column is the value that tells nodes apart (usually the primary key). No data is copied. Every time you run MATCH (n:PoLine) , the source erp.po_line is read. It is read-only . If you CREATE or SET on a virtual node, the engine refuses. To change values you have to change them in the source system, and in Ontological Studio that is the job of actions (Part 6). h: Sorting and limiting — ORDER BY · SKIP · LIMIT
x: Open Ontological Portal and run the basic Cypher clauses — MATCH, WHERE, RETURN, ORDER BY and LIMIT — one at a time on the sample data. Cypher: queries you draw Cypher is a query language that describes graph structure the way you would draw it . It started in Neo4j and is now the basis of GQL, the ISO standard graph query language. Picture Cypher Meaning ○ (s:Supplier) One node with the Supplier label, named s ○→○ (po)-[:ORDERED_FROM]->(s) An ORDERED_FROM relationship from po to s Property s.name The name value of node s It is easy to understand if you compare it with SQL's SELECT … FROM … WHERE . SQL Cypher FROM supplier s MATCH (s:Supplier) WHERE s.country = 'China' WHERE s.country = 'China' SELECT s.name RETURN s.name ORDER BY … LIMIT 3 ORDER BY … LIMIT 3 JOIN … ON … Relationship pattern -[:REL]-> ( Chapter 8 ) Opening the Portal On Home, click the Ontological Portal card. In the graph selector at the top left, choose sample . Every example in Part 4 runs on the sample graph. h: Keep rows without a match — OPTIONAL MATCH
x: Find nodes by following relationship patterns, connect several databases in one query, and summarize with count, sum and collect. This is where Cypher starts to feel easier than SQL. Relationship patterns po.po_id po.status s.name PO-001 OPEN Shenzhen Goldline PCB PO-002 OPEN Shenzhen Goldline PCB PO-003 CLOSED Hanbit Precision PO-004 CLOSED Daesung Cable PO-005 OPEN Ningbo Magnetics PO-006 OPEN Hanoi Assembly PO-007 OPEN Ningbo Magnetics PO-008 OPEN Hanbit Precision Purchase orders come from purchase_order in the ERP, and suppliers from supplier in the ERP. The relationship ORDERED_FROM replaces the join purchase_order.supplier_id = supplier.supplier_id . Direction Pattern Meaning (a)-[:R]->(b) From a to b (a)<-[:R]-(b) From b to a — the same relationship, read from the other end (a)-[:R]-(b) Either direction Every relationship has a defined direction ( PurchaseOrder → Supplier ). To start from the supplier, reverse the arrow. s.name orders Daesung Cable ["PO-004"] Shenzhen Goldline PCB ["PO-001", "PO-002"] Hanbit Precision ["PO-003", "PO-008"] Ningbo Magnetics ["PO-005", "PO-007"] Hanoi Assembly ["PO-006"] Put a label on every node In Ontological DB, queries are faster and more accurate when you write a label on every node in the pattern. Write (po:PurchaseOrder) instead of (s:Supplier)<-[:ORDERED_FROM]-(po) . In particular, if you look for a virtual relationship in the data fabric without labels, as -[r]-> (with no relationship name either), the result comes back empty. Make it a habit to write the relationship name and the labels on both ends. Several hops — across databases This is the question you saw in Chapter 3 : shipment (WMS) → purchase order (ERP) → supplier (ERP). sh.shipment_no sh.ship_status sh.delay_days po.po_id s.name SHP-03 CUSTOMS_HOLD 9 PO-002 Shenzhen Goldline PCB SHP-02 IN_TRANSIT 7 PO-001 Shenzhen Goldline PCB SHP-06 IN_TRANSIT 3 PO-005 Ningbo Magnetics SHP-05 DELIVERED 1 PO-004 Daesung Cable If you return whole nodes, you can view the result as a graph. Give the relationships variables too ( r , o ) and return them as well. For the same Cypher, this fingerprint stays the same even if you change the point in time (Chapter 10) — the query is the same, and only the conditions change. The fabric execution plan — EXPLAIN FABRIC When a query reaches sources in several databases, performance depends on which system runs which part of the work . Put EXPLAIN FABRIC in front of a query to see the plan step by step. step place operation rows detail 1 remote:erp join 8 SELECT r10.po_id, r12.name FROM (erp.purchase_order r10 INNER JOIN erp.supplier r12 ON …) 2 remote:wms scan 2 SELECT shipment_no, ref_po_no FROM wms.shipment WHERE ((delay_days > 3)) 3 local Hash Join 2 (purchase_order.po_id = (shipment.ref_po_no)::text) EXPLAIN FABRIC — the SQL sent to each source and the number of rows that came back How to read it: The join inside the ERP ran in the ERP (purchase order ⋈ supplier). Work within one database is left to that source. The WMS got the query with its condition ( delay_days > 3 ). Only 2 rows came back, not all 8. Ontological DB did only the last join, the one that links the two different databases. The more source data you have, the bigger this difference gets. If a condition cannot be pushed down to a source (for example, a condition that compares values from two databases), it shows up as local in the plan. x: “What was true back then?” and “What did we know back then?” are different questions. Learn the two time axes, and ask the same Cypher again with only the point in time changed. Why you need two times Say HR recorded Haneul Kim's salary like this: 4,000 from January 2021 — she joins the company. 4,600 from January 2024 — a raise. Her actual salary changed (a change). A few months later, HR finds that the 2024 raise was actually to 4,700 and fixes it. Her actual salary didn't change; the recorded number was wrong (a correction). Now an auditor asks: “What was her salary in June 2025?” The answer is 4,700. But if they ask, “Why did the report written before the correction say 4,600?”, you must be able to reproduce the value we knew at that time. Time axis What it asks Ontological DB setting Valid time When was it true in the real world? valid_at System time (record time) Since when have we recorded it that way? system_at (as known at) Data that has both axes is called bitemporal . Valid period and stored period for the same product — in the records before the correction, August 15 is SAFE; in the records after it was corrected to RISK from July 1, it is RISK Same query, different point in time In Ontological DB, you set the point in time separately from the query statement. You keep the Cypher as it is and change only “as of when” you look. Point-in-time query flow — for the same question, choose a valid date and a recorded-as-of time; the query finds the records that fit those dates (current, past, before correction) and answers with the information and relationships of that time The same point in time applies to relationships too. If you ask as of 2022, the query follows only the relationships that existed in 2022. When you ask about the present, only current rows are read; records from before a correction are searched only when you set a point in time. So everyday queries don't slow down even with a lot of history. h: Golden Questions — where design starts and how you know it's done
Golden Commands — where action design starts
The two ideas side by side
x: Two things you decide before you build an ontology — the questions it must answer and the things it must do . The build agent designs from them, and checks its work against them at the end. What is the ontology for? If you try to put every piece of information into an ontology, the build scope gets far too wide. So Ontological Studio asks you to write down three things before the build starts. Item Question Example from Supply Chain Operations (Sample) Build intent Who uses it, and to do what? Supply chain operators ask about late inbound shipments and quality problems, and ask the systems to expedite shipments, put purchase orders on hold and notify customers Golden Question A question this ontology must be able to answer Which inbound shipments are more than 3 days late, and which supplier and purchase order are they for? Golden Command An instruction this ontology must be able to carry out Expedite the inbound shipments that are more than 3 days late (reason: risk of production disruption) Build brief — build intent, 3 Golden Questions, 4 Golden Commands Where can I see the sample brief? In Build Ontology , choose Supply Chain Operations (Sample) (ingest more) as the target. The Intent step then shows the sample brief filled in (3 Golden Questions, 4 Golden Commands). If you choose Create new schema , you start from an empty brief. Golden Questions — where design starts and how you know it's done A Golden Question works like acceptance criteria in software engineering. When designing — the agent works backward from the question to find what's needed. From “which supplier and purchase order”, it knows it needs the Shipment , PurchaseOrder and Supplier classes and the relationships between them. This is called schema-first design . When validating — when the build is done, the agent runs the Golden Questions itself and checks that the expected answers and evidence come back. If not, it fixes the schema or the mappings and runs them again. When using it — they appear as example questions in the query screen and in ontology apps. Schema-first design and evidence-based iterative validation — from the intent and Golden Questions, build a candidate schema and a search path for each question, then analyze why results fall short and fill the gaps Writing good Golden Questions Weaker Better Why Tell me about the suppliers What are Shenzhen Goldline PCB's open purchase orders? The target and condition must be specific before you can validate the answer How's quality? Which customer's order did the PCB soldering defect claim come from? The shape of the answer (customer, order) is clear Shipments, purchase orders, suppliers Which inbound shipments are more than 3 days late, and which supplier and purchase order are they for? A question that follows several relationships confirms the schema path you need Write them as questions a real business user would ask out loud . If every question ends after one relationship, the schema stays shallow. Mix in questions that go through two or three relationships . Questions with exactly one right answer are best. They are easier to validate. Golden Commands — where action design starts A Golden Command is an acceptance criterion for doing something . For each Golden Command, the build agent: looks through the APIs (OpenAPI specs) of the registered business systems to find the API that carries out the instruction, pairs it with an API that undoes that work (compensation), adds a policy for who can use it on which targets, making it an action , and validates it with a dry run , which only makes a plan without actually executing anything. The sample's four Golden Commands and the actions built from them: Golden Command Action Execute (compensation) Expedite the inbound shipments that are more than 3 days late (reason: risk of production disruption) Shipment.expediteShipment WMS priority URGENT (back to the previous value) → ERP expedite request to the supplier (withdraw) Put all of Shenzhen Goldline PCB

Using the sample actions, you see how steps, argument mapping, compensation and policy fit together. What is an action? An action is a business operation defined on a class of the ontology. In the sample, the Shipment class has expediteShipment (expedite an inbound shipment). An action contains the following: Part Meaning In Shipment.expediteShipment Target key The property that identifies the target instance shipment_no Input Values a person (or the agent) gives when executing reason (reason for expediting, required) Steps The system APIs to call, in order ① WMS priority URGENT ② ERP expedite request to the supplier Compensation For each step, the API that undoes it ① priority back to the value before execution ② withdraw the expedite request Policy Who can use it, on which targets Role scm_operator ; shipments already received ( DELIVERED ) are excluded Approval Does it need a person's approval? In the sample, every plan needs approval Writeback The property written back to the ontology after execution priority Golden Command The instruction this action was built from “Expedite the inbound shipments that are more than 3 days late (reason: risk of production disruption)” Taking a definition apart Here is the definition of the sample action (descriptions shortened). Argument mapping — where do the values come from? On the left of arg_mapping is a slot in the API request ( path.… is the URL path, body.… is the request body). On the right is where the value comes from. Source Meaning Example $this.<property> A property of the target instance $this.shipment_no → SHP-03 $params.<name> An input given at execution $params.reason → “risk of production disruption” $actor.<claim> The person (or agent) who executed it $actor.sub → lite-agent $before.<property> The target's property value just before execution $before.priority → NORMAL $steps.<step>.response.<path> A value from an earlier step's API response $steps.erp.response.id → the expedite request number $cancel.reason The reason given when canceling “Expedite canceled at the user's request” A plain value A fixed value "URGENT" $before and $steps are what make compensation possible. To put the priority back, you need to know “what the original value was”; to withdraw an expedite request, you need to know “which request was sent”. Compensation doesn't erase things — it puts them back the way they were . Policy — who, and on what A policy is a list of rules. Each rule has roles ( roles ) and a condition ( when ). If any rule matches, the action is allowed; if none match, it is denied (deny by default). Conditions are written in a small expression language called CEL.
